title: How Entomophagy Works
summary: Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant discuss entomophagy, the practice of eating insects. They cover its history, citing the Bible (Leviticus permits locusts and certain beetles, and John the Baptist reportedly ate locusts and honeycomb), Greeks and Romans eating beetle larvae and locusts, and Aristotle eating cicadas. They note Aboriginal Australians eating grubs, which they say taste like roasted almonds, and that over 1,400 edible insect species exist, including about 350 beetle kinds. They discuss eating wasps and whether venom matters once cooked, and South American consumption of tarantulas and scorpions, with a quote from Peter Menzel's book Man Eating Bugs. They go through FDA Food Defect Action Levels, which allow insect fragments, rodent hairs and excreta in foods such as frozen broccoli, cinnamon, noodles, pepper and popcorn. They close with nutritional benefits of crickets and caterpillars (caterpillar protein comparable to salmon), precautions about collecting wild insects, and a rule of thumb that brightly colored or pungent insects are likely poisonous.

segments.title: Opening banter and introduction
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck introduce the episode, joking about eating bugs and Chuck's dinner-party idea of fried cricket. Josh asks about regional differences in eating insects.

segments.title: History of eating insects in the Bible and ancient world
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Old Testament food rules, noting that locusts and some beetles are permitted while rabbit, pigs and weasels are not. They mention John the Baptist eating locusts and honeycomb, Greeks and Romans eating beetle larvae and locusts, and Aristotle eating cicadas. Aboriginal Australians eating grubs is also mentioned.

segments.title: Edible insect species and eating wasps
segments.summary: Chuck says more than 1,400 edible insect species exist, including about 350 beetle kinds, and that ants, bees, wasps and butterflies are eaten. Wasps are usually prepared with wings and legs removed, roasted or boiled in soup. The hosts discuss whether venom matters once the insect is cooked.

segments.title: Cultural taboos and tarantulas in South America
segments.summary: The hosts note that around three thousand ethnic groups eat bugs and that food taboos are cultural. They compare it to lobsters and crabs. They mention South American consumption of tarantulas and scorpions and quote Peter Menzel's description of tarantula taste from Man Eating Bugs.

segments.title: FDA food defect action levels and insect fragments in food
segments.summary: Chuck describes the FDA's Food Defect Action Levels handbook, which sets acceptable levels of natural or unavoidable defects such as insect fragments, rodent hairs and excreta in foods like frozen broccoli, ground cinnamon, macaroni, pepper and popcorn. Josh and Chuck joke about these standards.

segments.title: Nutrition benefits and foraging safety
segments.summary: Chuck gives nutritional figures for crickets and caterpillars, with caterpillars offering protein comparable to salmon. The hosts discuss precautions for collecting wild insects, including pesticide risk in the US and cleaning insects by feeding them grass, and a rule of thumb that brightly colored or pungent insects are likely poisonous.

segments.title: Closing and sign-off
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck wrap up and invite listeners to read the related article on HowStuffWorks and to email feedback.
